description: 9-5 Dev and Tester from Vietnam who wants something cool
summary: Vanilla Sphere turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a blink comparator that runs in any browser. Pick a spot on the sky map, or type a position or a name, and it plays every SPHEREx image of that patch of sky as a short movie, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out. Nothing is pre-downloaded: the server finds every Level 2 exposure through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive and reads only the bytes it needs from NASA's public cloud copy, so any coordinate works. A blind search of each wide field links detections into tracks: with nothing known beforehand it found the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS and ten main-belt asteroids in three test fields, and every track it kept is a known object. A pipeline fits motions: for Epsilon Indi B it recovers 4.68 arcseconds per year, the Gaia value. From the same exposures the tool builds a 0.75 to 5.0 micron spectrum, says in plain sentences which bands and lines it shows and whether the object changed between visits, and reads a redshift off the emission lines of quasars: all 94 it gave in a test on 189 spectra are within 2 percent of the published value. Finding distant Solar System bodies and cold brown dwarfs takes many eyes on many fields, and Vanilla Sphere makes every field a link anyone can open and share.
details:
What it does

Vanilla Sphere is a blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx survey. Type coordinates or a name, and the tool gathers every SPHEREx exposure that covers that position and plays them in time order on one north-up grid. Stars stay still; anything that moves or varies catches the eye, the same principle Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto.

How it works

  1. Search. The server asks the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA Simple Image Access) which Level 2 spectral images cover the position.
  2. Read only what is needed. Each Level 2 file is about 65 MB and covers 3.5 by 3.5 degrees. Instead of downloading files, the server reads the header and only the pixel rows of the cutout from NASA's public cloud bucket with HTTP range requests: 1.3 to 1.9 MB per exposure for an 8 arcminute view. We verified that the result is identical, pixel for pixel, to a cutout made from the fully downloaded file.
  3. Clean and align. Flagged pixels are masked, the sky background is subtracted, and every exposure is resampled onto the same grid.
  4. Show. Frames are grouped per exposure, per day or per six-month sky pass. Results are cached, so a region that has been opened once reopens in a fraction of a second.

What you can do with it

  • Start from a sky map that opens on the centre of the Milky Way, with the 2MASS near-infrared atlas behind the drawn stars. Click any spot, or type coordinates or a name. A Simple mode serves newcomers and an Advanced mode has every control.
  • Watch a false-colour movie (red, green and blue from detectors 6, 4 and 2) or any single detector band from 0.75 to 5.0 microns. SPHEREx sees one position with only one or two detectors per day, so a missing colour channel is borrowed from the nearest date and marked on every frame.
  • Subtract the median of all frames or a chosen reference epoch so that static stars vanish, or add all frames together.
  • Survey a wider field: a progressive mode fills a block of 3×3 or 7×7 cells (up to 0.84 degrees) around the position, ring by ring.
  • Let the tool search for what moves. Once a wide field has loaded, a blind search links detections that shift between exposures into tracks, sorts them into fast and slow movers with speed and direction, and names those that are known asteroids or comets (SkyBoT, JPL). Each track opens the exposures it was seen in. Everything found goes into a public Discoveries log, where visitors can vote “real motion” or “false alarm”.
  • Read a spectrum built on the fly. Each exposure sees the target through a different slice of the linear variable filter, so the exposures together give a 0.75 to 5.0 micron spectrum. Under the plot a preliminary reading says in sentences what the curve shows: the continuum, absorption bands of water, methane, water ice and carbon dioxide, and emission lines of hydrogen and helium. Each sentence is a fixed test on the measured points, with its numbers and a confidence level; no language model is involved.
  • See whether it changed. The Over time plot groups the exposures by visit, and a line under it says whether the brightness changed, by how much, and in which bands.
  • See how far away it is: a distance from the Gaia parallax for stars; for galaxies and quasars the published redshift with its paper and how long the light has travelled. A layer on the sky map shows 10,037 galaxies and quasars by redshift, and up to six spectra can be compared in the rest frame. Where a spectrum shows emission lines, the tool also reads a redshift from the lines themselves and labels it as its own reading.
  • Overlay Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 sources, moved by their proper motion to the date of each frame.
  • See the positions and tracks our pipeline measured, next to the catalogue values, and spectra of bright stars that saturate the detector.
  • See the quality flags of the pixels under the target for every frame.
  • Share any view and take the data: the coordinates, field of view and settings live in the URL, an image API returns the same view as a PNG frame or an animated GIF, every plot saves as CSV or PNG with the NASA credit, and each exposure links to its Level 2 file at IRSA.

Results

All five targets named in the challenge load with no failed reads, 1,948 exposures in total: Barnard's Star (358), Epsilon Indi B (458), WISE 0855-0714 (258), RW Aurigae (335) and R Draconis (539). A measurement pipeline finds each target on the native detector pixels of every exposure and fits its motion. Barnard's Star moves 10.33 ± 0.25 arcseconds per year north, from 86 positions (Gaia DR3: 10.36). Epsilon Indi B moves +3945 ± 48 and −2513 ± 49 mas per year, from 431 positions (Gaia DR3: +3982 and −2467). WISE 0855-0714 is too faint for single exposures, so the exposures of each sky pass are added first; six such detections give −8.8 ± 1.0 and +1.5 ± 1.0 arcseconds per year, consistent with the published −8.12 and +0.67.

Moving objects, found blind. In three test fields along the path of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS (450 to 713 exposures each) the search kept 12 tracks, and every one is a known object: the comet in two fields, at 99.4 and 174.9 arcseconds per hour (IRSA's Moving Object Search Tool gives 99 and 168), and ten main-belt asteroids of visual magnitude 11.8 to 17.9. Repeating the search with the exposure times shuffled gave no chance tracks. To measure what the search misses, we added 1,440 artificial asteroids to the real exposures of three fields: it finds 85 and 87 percent of those brighter than visual magnitude 17.5 where stars are few or moderately many and 59 percent in a crowded field, and half are still found at magnitude 18.1 where stars are few (17.1 in the crowded field). An audit on a crowded field near Barnard's Star did find two false tracks, so a sighting now has to be a compact source, and a track that no catalogue explains is listed as a candidate, not as a discovery.

Slow, distant objects. A second search adds the frames of a sky pass together along the path a body beyond Neptune would follow, so that objects too slow or too faint for single exposures show up. The public Discoveries log lists three bodies found this way, each named afterwards by the catalogue: Pluto, Makemake and Orcus (visual magnitude 15.1, 17.1 and 19.1), with a rough distance read from the bend of the path. Tested on 529 artificial bodies placed 30 to 110 au from the Sun, it finds 73 percent of those brighter than visual magnitude 19 (236 of 325), and half are still found at magnitude 19.1. It needs a long pass: in passes shorter than 300 hours it found 5 of 41. None of the paths it reported was made of nothing.

Change over time. R Draconis, a pulsing red giant, is about 1.9 times fainter in June 2026 than in June 2025 (3.8 sigma). RW Aurigae changed colour: at 3.8 to 5.0 microns it was up to 2.0 times brighter in September 2025 than a year later (9.0 sigma), while at 0.74 to 1.6 microns it brightened up to 1.6 times (5.7 sigma), so the total stayed nearly steady. Of 17 objects not known to vary, none shows a change above 2.3 sigma in any band.

Redshift from the lines. On 189 SPHEREx spectra of quasars the tool gave a redshift for 94, and all 94 are within 2 percent of the published value in 1 + z. Half of that sample (89 spectra, 50 redshifts) was read only after the thresholds were fixed. On 35 stars, brown dwarfs and nebulae it gave none, as it should.

Speed and bright stars. A 7×7 survey of 49 cells (0.84 degrees, 580 to 735 exposures, 5.9 to 7.2 GB read from NASA's S3 bucket) completes in 37 to 52 seconds on first load with no failed frames, and reopens from cache in under 5 seconds; a new 8 arcminute view takes about 10 seconds. Stars brighter than about K = 9 saturate the core of SPHEREx images, so plain aperture photometry reads 2 to 5 times too low. Vanilla Sphere measures these stars from the halo of the point spread function, calibrated on 81 2MASS stars in 29,000 exposures: the result agrees with 2MASS to 20 to 25 percent from 0.15 to 20 Jy, and unsaturated stars agree to 2 to 4 percent. Barnard's Star has a spectrum point in 350 of its 358 exposures and R Draconis in 527 of 539. R Draconis at 4.3 to 4.9 microns falls from 64 to 50 to 33 Jy over three visits; it is brighter than the calibrated range, so its fluxes are relative only and are flagged EXTRAPOLATED.

Benefits and intended impact

A scientist or a citizen scientist can check any position in seconds without installing software, downloading tens of gigabytes or learning the archive's interfaces. Because nothing is pre-processed, the tool follows the archive: when NASA publishes a new SPHEREx release, adding its collection name is the only change needed. Every view is a link, so a candidate can be passed to a colleague or embedded in a report exactly as it was seen.

Tools

Python (FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, fsspec, Pillow) with an on-disk SQLite cache; a plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript viewer with no build step; hosted on Render in the US East region next to NASA's data bucket; a Supabase Postgres database for positions measured by the team.

What is creative about it

Most image tools copy the survey first. We read the archive's own files in place, a few rows at a time, which is what lets one small server cover the whole sky. The spectrum uses a property unique to SPHEREx: its filter varies across the detector, so a movie of one source is also its spectrum.

What we considered

Scientific honesty came first: one shared contrast stretch for all frames, quality flags always visible, borrowed colour channels labelled, and limits stated plainly (for example, WISE 0855 is too faint for single exposures and is measured only after the exposures of a sky pass are added, and fluxes of stars brighter than the calibrated range are flagged as relative). We also weighed speed for a first-time visitor, hosting cost, and use on a phone.

Use of AI tools

We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as a coding and writing assistant. It wrote most of the source code and tests under the team's direction and review, helped research the SPHEREx data access path, helped design the interface, ran the timing and pixel-comparison checks, and helped draft and translate this submission and the slides. No AI model runs inside the product: every image shown is NASA data processed by deterministic code. No images, video or audio were AI-generated.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Level 2 Spectral Images (DR1, QR3), NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive
IRSA Cloud Data Access: SPHEREx on AWS Open Data (bucket nasa-irsa-spherex)
CatWISE2020 Catalog (NASA WISE/NEOWISE), queried through IRSA TAP
2MASS All-Sky Point Source Catalog and colour atlas (NASA/NSF), through IRSA: calibration of bright-star photometry and the backdrop of the sky map
IRSA Moving Object Search Tool (MOST), used to check the tracks of moving objects against JPL ephemerides
JPL Small-Body Identification API (NASA/JPL Solar System Dynamics), names of known asteroids and comets
projectRefs: ESA Gaia Data Release 3 (queried through IRSA TAP)
SIMBAD astronomical database, CDS Strasbourg (name lookup, published redshifts and distances)
Claude and Claude Code by Anthropic (AI assistant, see Use of AI tools)
SkyBoT, IMCCE / Paris Observatory (names of known asteroids and comets)
VizieR, CDS Strasbourg (two published quasar composite spectra, used as a template)
NIST Atomic Spectra Database (reference wavelengths of spectral lines)
d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD 3-Clause): star, constellation and Milky Way data of the sky map
